content:
Offering less than 35 miles of range and a 40 mph top speed from its 9.5 kW electric motor and 4.3 kWh lead-acid battery pack, the Volvo Elbil made was a far cry from the company’s cutting-edge EX60 – but when it made its debut in November 1976? The Elbil concept was the start of something much bigger than itself.
When Volvo rolled the Elbil out of its Gothenburg skunkworks in 1976, it didn’t just break from nearly fifty years of internal combustion history – the Elbil also broke from Volvo’s tradition of naming its concepts after Swedish name days. Earlier Volvo concept cars and design studies carried names like Philip and Margarete Rose, inspired by Sweden’s tradition of assigning a name to every day of the calendar. With the Elbil, Volvo went literal: Elbil means “electric car” in Swedish.
Very electric, Very car
![](https://electrek.co/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/11/volvo-elbil-concept-1976-yellow-copy.jpg?quality=82&strip=all)
Riding a steel skateboard and featuring lightweight composite and aluminum body panels, the ’76 EV built around twelve, 6V car batteries, the tiny Elbil was built as a low-cost runabout for young Swedes that prized practicality over power and performance. The car’s sliding composite doors, parts bin seas, and flat glass with pop-out side window vents replacing the rolly up-and-down type all helped keep the near-production concept’s costs and weight at manageable levels, and served to give it a distinctive Volvo box-era look.
Alas, despite a relatively high level of refinement and a ready customer in Sweden’s state-owned telecom company Televerket, the Elbil concept never made it to Volvo showrooms. Only two were built in the end (the orange and yellow Elbil shown, above), and it would be another decade before Volvo tried its hand at EVs again – in the form of a one-off Volvo 480 Electric coupe with 120 km (about 60 miles) of range.
Today, the company is very different. Now owned by Chinese automaker Geely, Volvo committed itself to offering only electric and electrified vehicles all the way back in 2017; and they’ve held true to that commitment (more than others, anyway).
“The Elbil was a bold example of Volvo’s forward-thinking approach to electrification, demonstrating our ambition to explore new technologies long before electric vehicles became mainstream,” commented Nicole Melillo Shaw, Managing Director Volvo Car UK. “Fifty years on, the EX60 shows just how far we’ve come, combining exceptional electric range, rapid charging and pioneering safety innovations … while the technology has evolved significantly, what we stand for remains unchanged – to develop cars that make life easier, safer and better for people.”
